articles.title: Your Free AI Lane Is Slow in the Queue, Not in the Model
articles.excerpt: You moved a batch to free capacity. The token bill dropped to zero. The deadline still slipped. Nothing in the model got slower. The jobs sat in a queue you never charted. Most AI cost dashboards star…
articles.body: You moved a batch to free capacity. The token bill dropped to zero. The deadline still slipped. Nothing in the model got slower. The jobs sat in a queue you never charted. Most AI cost dashboards start counting at the first token. That is the wrong start line for a free lane. On free capacity, the wall clock usually belongs to scheduling, not to generation. This post is a drill, not a vendor pitch. You record two clocks per job. Then you run one script and get a verdict: hold the batch, or spill it to paid capacity before the cutoff. Start the clock at enqueue, not at first token Your job record needs five timestamps. Anything less and you cannot separate waiting from working. enqueue_ts — the job was accepted by your scheduler. start_ts — the first request hit the serving path.

articles.body: Pollen Robotics Open-Sources a 25cm, 800g Reinforcement-Learning Robot Duck Pollen Robotics, the Hugging Face-backed open-source robotics company, has released Microduck: a bipedal robot just 25cm tall and 800g in weight whose walking, recovery, and object-manipulation skills are trained largely through reinforcement learning rather than hand-coded motion. Both the robot's runtime and its RL training pipeline are now open source, making Microduck one of the smallest fully open embodied-AI development platforms on the market — and a compact reference implementation for an entire stack: MuJoCo simulation, PPO training, Sim2Real transfer, ONNX export, and real-time control in Rust.

articles.title: Five Fail-Closed Gates, One Script: Rehearse Your AI Feature on a Free Tier First
articles.excerpt: My readiness checklist for small AI features is a Markdown file. It has nine boxes and zero exit codes. Nobody has opened it since August. That is the whole problem. A checklist you read is a wish. A…
articles.body: My readiness checklist for small AI features is a Markdown file. It has nine boxes and zero exit codes. Nobody has opened it since August. That is the whole problem. A checklist you read is a wish. A checklist you run is a gate. So I rewrote mine as one script. It runs in about two seconds. It exits non-zero when anything is wrong. And it runs first against a deliberately broken fake model, not against a real one. Here is the harness, the evidence it writes, and the limits of rehearsing on a free tier. The gate is not the model call Most teams test the model. Few test the guard around the model. Ask yourself: if the model returned truncated JSON right now, what happens? Does your service crash, show a blank card, or quietly bill you twice?

articles.title: I Bisected My Prompt Until the Endpoint Broke
articles.excerpt: Last Tuesday I tried to turn a 40-minute lecture transcript into study questions. I pasted it into a chat box, pressed send, and got back a red error that told me almost nothing. Not "your input is 61…
articles.body: Last Tuesday I tried to turn a 40-minute lecture transcript into study questions. I pasted it into a chat box, pressed send, and got back a red error that told me almost nothing. Not "your input is 61,000 characters." Not "too long for this model." Just a failure, and a cursor blinking at me like it knew something I didn't. So I did what students do. I guessed. I cut the transcript in half, pasted again, then in half again, and spent eleven minutes doing arithmetic with my eyes. Then it hit me — why am I acting as the bisection algorithm? That's a loop I can write in fifteen lines. This is the story of that loop, what it measured, and the one number I now refuse to hardcode.

articles.title: Capacity You Haven't Measured Is Capacity You Don't Have
articles.excerpt: At 2 a.m. on a Thursday, a demo I had rehearsed four times died on the first request, in front of six people, on a free server I had never once looked inside. The endpoint answered locally. The migrat…
articles.body: At 2 a.m. on a Thursday, a demo I had rehearsed four times died on the first request, in front of six people, on a free server I had never once looked inside. The endpoint answered locally. The migration ran on my laptop. The only thing that had changed was the box, and I had no number for that box, no memory ceiling, no cold-start figure, no idea whether the disk could take an eight-megabyte write. So here is my position, and I will argue it rather than hedge it: capacity you have not measured is capacity you do not have, and a free tier is only useful to the degree that you interrogate it. That sounds like a complaint about free infrastructure, and it is not.

articles.title: How OpenVTS engineered whole-fleet live tracking without freezing""How OpenVTS engineered whole-fleet live tracking without freezing
articles.excerpt: A live fleet map feels magical at 30 vehicles. It feels broken at 3,000. The same map, the same code, the same server — and suddenly the markers stutter, the tab chews through memory, the browser warn…
articles.body: A live fleet map feels magical at 30 vehicles. It feels broken at 3,000. The same map, the same code, the same server — and suddenly the markers stutter, the tab chews through memory, the browser warns "page unresponsive," and dispatchers stop trusting what they see. Nothing crashed. It just stopped being live . The instinct is to blame the map library. The real cause is almost always the pipeline feeding it: how position updates travel from thousands of devices to thousands of screens, and how much work gets repeated on every single packet. OpenVTS is a self-hosted GPS tracking and fleet-management platform.

Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. An Anticrepuscular Rainbow Fan Explanation: This is an unusual rainbow. For one thing, the rainbow is not complete, appearing only in a sunlit fan — but that by itself is not very unusual. What is most unusual is the fake location of the Sun . The Sun appears to be toward the front, just below those hills — but it is not. That is not how rainbows work . Rainbows involve a backward reflection from falling rain , so that the Sun must really be behind you .

articles.excerpt: Brick by brick ... the truth is out there. You can now own a little piece of that with this 1,478-piece Lego set
articles.body: Millennials get a lot of flak for being overly nostalgic, but I don't think that's fair. When the modern-day world has nothing to offer us but AI slop, shrinkflation and a sad acceptance that we can't be bothered to do anything about global warming. It's easy to see why we yearn for the days of Pogs, the Backstreet Boys, and Saved by the Bell. One area that we definitely had it good in the 90s was sci-fi , when legendary shows like Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stargate SG-1, and — of course — The X-Files ruled our TV screens long before the age of streaming services . You can relive those glory days of alien conspiracies, spooky happenings and cell phones the size of a brick with the Lego Ideas The X-Files set.

articles.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
articles.excerpt: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment remini…
articles.body: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.
